```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

This is a guide to package arguments, array shapes and result fields. Start
with [Getting started](getting-started.html) for an analysis you can run.
For the statistical setup, assumptions and derivations, see the accompanying
[paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z).

## Localization and DNN conventions

`X` is an `n`-by-`p` matrix of localization covariates. Use `x0` for a
length-`p` profile or `X0` for an `m`-by-`p` matrix with one profile per row.
Supply exactly one target argument. In a data-frame call, `x_cols` selects
and orders the coordinates; targets must follow that order.

Reporting coordinates can be a subset of the covariates used by an external
nuisance learner. Keep nuisance predictions aligned with the training rows,
even if the learner used additional covariates.

### Kernel order `s` and neighbor count `k`

- `s` is the subsample order. Larger `s` gives tighter localization.
- `k` counts neighbors inside each subsample; the default is `k = 1`.
- `s` does not count retained full-sample neighbors. Exact weight support
  reaches rank `n - s + k` (`n - s + 1` at the default `k = 1`).
- Jackknife uncertainty needs `s < n`; estimate-only fits can use `s = n`.

When omitted, `s` follows `tuning_dnn_paper()` with multiplier `lambda = 0.4`.
[Kernel-order tuning](kernel-order-tuning.html) explains explicit orders and
candidate grids. [DNN weights](dnn-weights.html) covers rank and weight output.
The paper gives the theoretical scope of the default construction.

### Weights and effective sample size

`W` has observations in rows and targets in columns. For normalized weights,
`ess`, `neff` and diagnostic `n_eff` all mean `1 / sum(w^2)`. This measures
weight concentration; it is not a count of nonzero weights or a distance
radius. For NP/TDNN and CATE, `nobs(fit)` instead counts training observations.
TDNN can have signed weights, so positive-weight overlap interpretations do
not carry over to it.

### Numerical geometry and covariance

Saved prediction reuses the fitted training geometry. Fast jackknife
calculations also freeze it; legacy NP/TDNN/CATE `jackknife = "loo"` refits
sample-dependent geometry for each deletion. The two calculations can differ.
See `?distance_mahalanobis` for the fitted metric and rank-deficient cases.
Numerical engine details belong to the maintainer reference linked from
[CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Matrix and data-frame interfaces

| Quantity | Data-frame input | Matrix/vector input |
|---|---|---|
| Localization covariates | `data`, `x_cols` | `X` |
| Reporting profiles | `x0` or `X0` | `x0` or `X0` |
| Regression outcome | `y_col` or `y` | `Y` |
| CATE signal | nuisance column names or `pseudo_outcome` | `pseudo_outcome` |
| PLQR regressors | `D_cols` | `D` |
| PLQR nuisances | `g_col`, `mD_cols`, `density_col` | `g`, `mD`, `density` |

Tibbles use the data-frame route. Column selection is explicit; the package
does not guess variable names. These equivalent calls use a data frame
with numeric `X1`, `X2` and `Y` columns:

```{r interface-grammar}
df <- np_demo_data(n = 60, p = 2, seed = 1)$data
fit_table <- np_dnn(data = df, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", x0 = c(0, 0))
fit_matrix <- np_dnn(X = as.matrix(df[c("X1", "X2")]), Y = df$Y, x0 = c(0, 0))
all.equal(coef(fit_table), coef(fit_matrix))
```

## Estimator targets and signals

| Function | Supplied input beyond covariates/targets | Main result |
|---|---|---|
| `np_dnn()` | Outcome or scalar signal | `mu`: conditional mean |
| `np_tdnn()` | Outcome and two orders `s1 < s2` | `mu`: signed two-scale regression estimate |
| `cate_dnn()` | AIPW nuisance predictions or supplied pseudo-outcome | `tau`: conditional treatment effect |
| `clate_dnn()` | Outcome, binary instrument/treatment and five nuisance predictions | `theta`: conditional complier effect; paired `components` |
| `affine_ratio_dnn()` | Numerator and denominator signals | `theta`: ratio of local averages |
| `plqr_dnn()` | Regressors, nuisance predictions and `theta_eval` | `moment` at the supplied coefficient |
| `gmm_dnn()` | A moment model and its data/nuisances | Solved `theta` and convergence diagnostics |

A **score** is an observation-level contribution. A **moment** is its local
weighted average. The experimental PLQR wrapper evaluates a moment; it does
not solve for a coefficient. Experimental GMM does solve a moment problem.

## CATE nuisance conventions

For AIPW, supply `y_col`, `t_col`, `m0_col`, `m1_col` and `e_col`: outcome,
binary treatment, control mean, treated mean and treatment propensity.
Alternatively supply `pseudo_outcome`, which is used unchanged and is the
CATE route for matrix inputs. Nuisance models are fitted outside the package.

Propensities must be finite and in `[0, 1]`. The AIPW route clips them to
`[clip, 1 - clip]`, with default `clip = 1e-8`; clipping does not establish
overlap. A supplied signal alone cannot supply treatment-overlap diagnostics.
Earlier pooled-mean `m_col` inputs have been removed; both arm means are
required for AIPW. See the [migration guidance](getting-started.html#migrating-earlier-cate-inputs).

## CLATE conventions

`A` is the binary instrument and `D` is treatment. The five predictions
`e`, `m_y0`, `m_y1`, `m_d0`, `m_d1` are the instrument propensity and
outcome/treatment means in each **instrument arm**. `one_sided = TRUE`
selects the structural restriction that treatment is unavailable without
assignment; it permits omitting `m_d0`. Observing `D <= A` does not by itself
justify that restriction.

`iv_augmented_signals()` constructs paired outcome and treatment signals.
The fit divides their common-weight local averages. Augmented treatment
signals may be negative and are not compliance indicators. See the
[CLATE guide](conditional-late.html) for complete calls and
[paired inference](conditional-late-inference.html) for covariance and status
outputs. Ordinary residualized IV need not have the same causal target.

## Experimental PLQR target and nuisance conventions

All PLQR interfaces remain experimental. `theta_eval` is supplied by the user;
`theta` repeats it. The principal inputs are:

| Input | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `D` | Partially linear regressors |
| `g` | Nonparametric shape nuisance; not the entire conditional quantile |
| `mD` | Conditional means used to residualize the regressors |
| `density` | Conditional outcome density at the model threshold |

The package does not fit those nuisances or solve a local coefficient root.
See [Experimental PLQR](conditional-z-estimation.html) for calls and
`?plqr_dnn` for the full contract.

## Moment diagnostics versus coefficient inference

PLQR uncertainty has two distinct scales:

| Output | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `moment_se`, `moment_vcov` | Uncertainty of the localized moment |
| `theta_se`, `theta_vcov` | Density-backed coefficient sandwich output |
| `theta_omega` | `theta_vcov` multiplied by `neff` |

Coefficient intervals require `density`/`density_col`. Without it,
`moment_se` is a diagnostic and does not support `confint()` or prediction
intervals for coefficients. With density, `theta_meat = "analytic"` uses
score covariance; `theta_meat = "jackknife"` uses joint moment covariance.
These calculations do not turn a supplied coefficient into an estimated root.

## Experimental GMM conventions

`gmm_dnn()` uses a `gmm_model` to solve local moments and returns its own
coefficient covariance and convergence diagnostics. Its `J` is an
overidentification statistic; PLQR's `J`/`jacobian` is a derivative matrix.
See [Local IV estimation](local-iv-estimation.html) for the experimental GMM
workflow.

## Reading fitted objects

Stored fields and available methods differ by estimator:

| Class | Estimate fields | Uncertainty |
|---|---|---|
| `np_result` / `tdnn_np_result` | `mu` | `se`; joint target covariance from `vcov()` |
| `cate_result` | `tau` | `se`; joint target covariance from `vcov()` |
| `affine_ratio_result` / `clate_result` | `theta`, `components` | `se`, `component_vcov`, `theta_vcov` |
| `plqr_result` | `moment`, supplied `theta_eval` | Moment- and coefficient-scale fields above |
| `gmm_result` | Solved `theta` | `se`, `vcov` |

CATE and NP/TDNN covariance uses common deleted observations across targets
and requires an active fitted jackknife. It is calculated from retained
state, including serialized fits without optional extras. Both axes follow
`coef()` order. Prespecified contrasts still need the corresponding joint
inference assumptions.

CLATE covariance lists are marginal across targets. `component_vcov[[j]]` is
the paired two-by-two component covariance and `theta_vcov[[j]]` is the ratio
variance. These are already on the estimator scale: do not divide by `neff`
again. `theta_omega[[j]]` instead equals `neff[j] * theta_vcov[[j]]`.

`return` extras such as `W`, `dx`, `ess` and `tuning` add retained information
without changing the main estimate. Use `summary()`, `coef()`, `confint()`,
`predict()` and `diagnostics()` as documented for the fitted class. Missing
uncertainty remains missing. Finite ratio estimates can have unavailable
Wald intervals; inspect `status` and `wald_available` before reporting them.

Saved objects retain observation-level numeric inputs, outcomes or signals;
apply the underlying data's sharing restrictions. [Diagnostics and reporting](diagnostics-reporting.html)
and [visualisation](visualising-fits.html) cover inspection and presentation.
Intervals are pointwise; none of these output conventions establishes the
paper's assumptions or simultaneous confidence bands.
